« Hood Heroes », épisode 19 : Abdul Razi: “Hood Heroes,” Episode 19: Abdul Raziq Khan, chef at Mama Khan, the restaurant that feeds those in need
Bien plus qu’un simple restaurant famili: Much more than just a family-run Pakistani restaurant, Mama Khan is a place of solidarity where people fight food insecurity.
Abdul Raziq Khan, cofondateur de cet éta: Abdul Raziq Khan, co-founder of the restaurant, which is named in honour of his mother. Photo: Aude Simon
Ces dernières semaines ont été marquées: The past few weeks have been marked by heavy news that has weighed on our spirits. In La Converse’s newsroom, there have been few reasons to celebrate. So it was with great pleasure that I discovered Mama Khan’s Instagram profile, which immediately brought back my smile and my motivation.
Aujourd’hui, je suis très contente de vo: Today, I’m very happy to introduce you to Abdul Raziq, co-founder of Mama Khan, a family-run Pakistani restaurant whose team also works to help those with the least.
Abdul rêvait de devenir travailleur soci: Abdul dreamed of becoming a social worker, but after a few setbacks in his studies, he decided to go into the restaurant business while developing charitable initiatives: for three years now, every Friday, Mama Khan has been handing out free meals to people in need. When we met, about sixty takeout containers were already ready to be filled, simply waiting for the day’s dish to finish cooking.
Abdul a aussi créé un programme de ticke: Abdul also created a meal ticket program that lets recipients leave with a free meal. His goal is to give out 1,500 free meals. He’s already at 1,100 and, once he reaches his target, he intends to aim for 2,000 meals.
Le jeune homme que nous rencontrons semb: The young man we meet seems, to say the least, motivated. Yet he went through difficult times in his youth. “I’ve seen both sides of the street,” he tells us with a certain discretion. Today, he is a model of generosity and perseverance. His journey shows that it’s possible to change things, no matter where you come from, as long as you commit with determination.

<strong>Vendredi 14 février 2025.</stron: Friday, February 14, 2025. While storefronts across the city are decked out with bouquets of flowers and boxes of chocolates, a different kind of love is being shared on Saint-Denis Street. At Mama Khan, there are no candlelit dinners or romantic declarations, just about sixty takeout containers carefully opened, ready to receive the dish of the day: rice, salad and chickpeas.
Malgré la fermeture temporaire du restau: Although the restaurant has been temporarily closed because of the deaths of Abdul Raziq Khan’s father and aunt, he, his mother and his childhood friend Thanver Hossain are busy, as they have been every Friday for three years, feeding those who need it.
« Nous sommes fermés depuis deux mois, m: “We’ve been closed for two months, but on Fridays we keep handing out food,” begins Abdul Raziq, who is 29. His black beanie pulled down on his head and his dark hoodie contrast with his jovial personality and bright smile.
Ce vendredi, comme chaque semaine, ils p: This Friday, as every week, they hit the road to hand out free meals to those with the least. Today, the meeting point is Parc station.
Né et ayant grandi à Parc-Extension, Abd: Born and raised in Parc-Extension, Abdul has always known that food could be a way to build social bonds. Yet the path that led him to Mama Khan wasn’t a straight one. Before putting on the apron, he worked in very different jobs, including nightclub bouncer and security guard.
Mais derrière ces expériences, un rêve r: But behind those experiences, one dream remained rooted in him: becoming a social worker. “I wanted to become a social worker, but you had to go to McGill, and I wasn’t the smartest at school,” he says. When he realized that path was closed to him, he decided to do things differently: create a space where social assistance comes through meals. “When I opened the restaurant, I knew that, for me, the best way to help the community was to give food.”
<strong>Donner à la communauté et lutter: Giving back to the community and fighting food waste
« C’est bizarre pour un restaurant de re: “It’s weird for a restaurant to give back, I know,” Abdul Raziq acknowledges with a shrug. “But the truth is, at the end of the day, there’s always food left over. So instead of throwing it out, we put it in containers and give it to the community.”
Chaque soir, avant même que les portes n: Every evening, before the doors even close, the unserved dishes are redistributed. “It’s a hot meal, a real plate, prepared with the same care as for any other customer.”
Un mur couvert de tickets jaunes au fond: A wall covered in yellow tickets at the back of the dining room is a testament to that generosity. It’s the “Mama Khan Paid for This” program. Since it began, more than 1,100 meals have been given out. But Abdul has no intention of stopping there. “Maybe we’ll hit 2,000 this year.”
L’idée lui est venue à force d'observer: The idea came to him from watching people experiencing homelessness come into the restaurant and ask seated customers for spare change. The scene repeated itself so many times that Abdul understood he had to find a solution. “There’s a real problem on Saint-Denis. A lot of people are homeless. So I asked myself: ‘What can we do?’”
La réponse s’est imposée d’elle-même : o: The answer came naturally: offer free meal tickets hung on the restaurant wall. The principle is simple: anyone in need can walk in, take down a ticket and receive a hot meal, no questions asked.
« Les clients peuvent faire un don de ci: “Customers can donate five dollars to provide a meal to people in need. But since we’re a restaurant, it’s not easy to always ask people to contribute, so generally, we pay out of our own pocket,” Abdul explains.
Avec ces tickets-repas, les personnes da: With these meal tickets, people in need no longer have to beg. “I wanted it to be anonymous, simple, with no need to justify anything. All you have to do is show up with your ticket to get the meal, because everyone deserves to eat.”
Chaque jour, cinq ou six personnes vienn: Every day, five or six people come to pick up a meal, Abdul says. “It doesn’t sound like a lot, but if you do the math, every Tuesday to Sunday, after two or three months, that adds up to 200 to 300 meals given out.”
<strong>La foi comme carburant : donner: Faith as fuel: giving without expecting anything in return
Lorsqu’on demande à Abdul Raziq si donne: When asked whether giving away so much food has put Mama Khan in a difficult position, Abdul Raziq doesn’t stop to think before answering: “Probably, totally, for sure!” But right away, his smile widens. “The truth is, I’m Muslim. And in my faith, we believe that every good deed is its own reward.”
Depuis la mort de son père, le 17 septem: Since his father’s death on September 17, Abdul has redoubled his efforts. “Everything I do today, I do for him.” For the chef, giving is synonymous with neither loss nor sacrifice. “What have I really lost? Nothing. I fed someone, I helped someone, that’s all.”
Et avec le ramadan qui approche, Mama Kh: And with Ramadan approaching, Mama Khan is preparing a special initiative: offering free meals to single-parent families and widows. “A single mother, a person going through a hard time can contact us on Instagram or by email, and a volunteer will bring them a meal.”
Un autre projet lui tient également beau: Another project is also very close to his heart: a free halal school meal program. “One in five children in Quebec goes to school without a lunch. That’s huge!” he exclaims.
Abdul ne peut s’empêcher de penser à ses: Abdul can’t help thinking about his former classmates. “I used to see them, they had nothing to eat all day, I remember them. And I also remember the kid I was. I was neither poor nor rich, my parents did everything they could for me and gave me two dollars every day so I could buy myself a lunch and a snack.” During his CEGEP years, those two dollars were enough to feed him. “A cookie was barely 50 cents, and anyway, I couldn’t eat much, because in 2010 there really weren’t any halal options.”
Un constat qui demeure d’actualité dans: A reality that still holds true in community canteens. “They don’t offer halal meals, which inevitably excludes many Muslim children,” Abdul laments. Through his ambitious program, the chef fully intends to reduce that disparity.
Si Mama Khan survit et continue à aider: If Mama Khan survives and continues to help hundreds of people every month, it is neither thanks to the Quebec government nor thanks to any institutional support.
« Aucun fonds, rien. Je ne reçois pas un: “No funding, nothing. I don’t get a single cent from the government,” says Abdul, without anger but with a hint of weariness: because it is a restaurant and not a non-profit organization, it is ineligible for public grants. He relies instead on organizations such as Islamic Relief, private donors and his community.
Et le plus ironique dans tout ça ? S’il: And the most ironic part of all this? Although he receives no help, he was still reprimanded by the Quebec government. “I had problems with the CAQ because the free meal tickets the restaurant was handing out were written in English. Someone reported us to the government, and I got a letter forbidding us from offering free meals… with tickets written in English.” The Quebec government required him to translate the tickets into French, under threat of penalties. For three weeks, the program was therefore suspended while new meal tickets were printed.
« On n’avait pas réalisé que même un sim: “We hadn’t realized that even a simple scrap of paper like that had to be in French or bilingual. It wasn’t intentional, we just wanted to help.”
« On fait des erreurs, on nous le dit, o: “We make mistakes, we’re told, we fix them – that’s all.” He shrugs and sketches a smile. Neither the lack of funding nor even administrative obstacles will stop him.
« T’as pas besoin d’un papier pour savoi: “You don’t need a piece of paper to know what you can do or who you are.” Abdul says these words with assurance. “I wanted to help others. Today, I do it through Mama Khan, and maybe even more than if I had followed my original plan of becoming a social worker.”
Pour lui, tout part de l’action : « Fais: For him, everything starts with action: “Do what you have to do. Look, I’m from Parc-Extension. I never would have believed I’d have a business on Saint-Denis Street one day!”
Le jeune homme sait également combien le: The young man also knows how merciless the streets of neighbourhoods like Parc-Extension can be. “Whether you’re a ‘good kid’ or a ‘bad kid,’ sooner or later, you can get caught up in trouble.” He stays vague about his past, but warns: “I’ve seen both sides of the street. Trust me, you don’t want to end up in prison or dead.”
Alors, il insiste sur ce qu’il aurait ai: So he emphasizes what he would have liked to hear at their age: youth organizations exist, go to them. Hold on to whatever can help you grow. Abdul isn’t trying to give grand lectures. Just one piece of advice, a sincere warning. “I come from the street, from Parc-Ex. What you’re going through now, I went through it. Stay true to yourselves.”
Aujourd’hui, les dons de Mama Khan fonct: Today, Mama Khan’s donations run on the generosity of those who believe in its mission, but also on the restaurant’s own funds and, very often, on the personal resources of Abdul and his family. Yet helping can take the form of the simplest and smallest gesture, he reminds us: “If you want to support us, it’s easy: talk about us. Like, share, spread the word.”
Sur ces mots, Abdul se lève et disparaît: With that, Abdul gets up and disappears into the kitchen. A few moments later, he reappears, a large steaming pot in his hands. His friend lifts the lid and, without waiting, starts filling the containers lined up near the entrance.
« On ne met pas de viande, car dans Parc: “We don’t put in any meat, because in Parc-Extension, many people are Hindu and prefer a vegan option,” Abdul explains. “Every detail counts so that no one is left out.”
